Summary
Data source overview: Anders Sandberg’s speculative essay “We, Borg” analyses the psychology, sociology and technology of future high-bandwidth ‘hive-mind’ (borganism) collectives. It identifies multiple failure modes—memetic infection, group-think, communication scaling limits, and social parasitism—and proposes cybernetic design principles (immune-like meme defences, protected dissent channels, scalable topologies, unit accountability) together with concrete architectural mechanisms (arbitration layers, market-based bandwidth allocation, audit logging, symbiotic meme complexes).

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[79]
The paper is highly conceptual; many links are theoretical rather than empirically validated. All core causal-interventional pathways referenced are captured and inter-connected; edges that rely on inference are flagged with lower confidence. JSON structure and node naming obey the specification.

Inference-strategy justification
Where the author hinted at mechanisms (e.g. “integrate symbiotic replicators as immune system”) I treated these as design rationales and implementation mechanisms; explicit practical steps (e.g. “keep accountability of units”) were elevated to intervention nodes. Moderate inference (confidence ≤ 2) was used only to bridge clearly implied steps (e.g. mapping group-psychology findings to a protected-dissent protocol).

Extraction completeness explanation
Four separate risk areas are covered; each is traced through problem analysis, insight, rationale, mechanism, evidence and finally to an actionable intervention. Shared nodes (e.g. arbitration layer) connect the four strands into one integrated knowledge fabric with no isolated nodes.

Key limitations
• Empirical validation is weak in the source; many edge confidences are therefore low-medium.  
• Technical feasibility details (latency, compression ratios, security) are speculative and could not be decomposed further without external information.  
• Some framework names (e.g. “arbitration layer”) are author-specific; future sources may describe identical ideas with different terms—ontology harmonisation will be required at scale.
